full_text:
Gritters have laid more than 200 tonnes of tar and chipping to prevent roads from melting in heatwave weather conditions.
Cornwall Council's highways engineering firm Cormac said it had attended up to four incidents of road surfaces melting in the county due to the recent high temperatures.
Network manager Steve Bayley said crews were proactively out surface dressing to help roads which were "potentially vulnerable to the heat".
He said teams had carried out "quite a few kilometres" of surface dressing in the last month, even if it felt "odd" to see a gritter out at this time of year.
During the process, the road is sprayed with bitumen binder before stone chippings are spread onto this and pressed into the surface by a rollers.
"We're doing some proactive treatment in most cases because we're out there doing surface dressing which most people refer to as tar and chippings," Bayley said.
"While that's freshly laid, it can be quite vulnerable to that temperature, so we go down and actively spread 3mm (0.11 inches) gritter dust - sort of crushed stone - to try and stay on top of that temperature and stabilise the material."
Bayley said the loose chippings were left on the road to protect surface treatment, and when they had been bedded in, the roads were swept two or three times to remove the excess.
The work can only take place during warm periods of the day to be "effective".
He added: "We've been much more on the case this year in terms of proactivity to get to the point where we're preventing it becoming a problem."

Dubai: August is expected to bring another month of intense summer weather across the UAE, with high temperatures, rising humidity and the continued likelihood of afternoon convective clouds and rainfall in some areas, according to the National Center of Meteorology (NCM).

Combined with intense daytime heating and the eastern mountain range, these conditions encourage the formation of convective clouds that can produce afternoon showers, particularly over the eastern regions before extending to parts of the interior.
During the first half of the month, parts of the UAE may also be affected by the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), which can enhance the development of rain-bearing clouds.
NCM said local wind patterns will continue to shape daily weather conditions, with south-easterly winds prevailing overnight and during the morning before shifting to northerly winds during the day.
At times, active southerly winds in the morning may raise dust, while north-westerly winds are also expected to strengthen intermittently.
Humidity is forecast to increase slightly compared with July, particularly during the second half of August, with average relative humidity reaching around 47 per cent, making conditions feel more uncomfortable during the morning and evening hours.
According to the NCM's August climate report, the month's average temperature typically ranges between 34.7C and 36.5C, while average daytime highs range from 40.9C to 43.2C and average overnight lows from 29.3C to 31C.
Average wind speeds are expected to be around 12kph, although historical records show the strongest wind gust recorded during August reached 127.8kph in Al Hayer in 2023.
The report also highlights the UAE's climatic extremes during August. Maximum relative humidity generally ranges between 63 and 80 per cent, while the highest rainfall ever recorded during the month was 100.4mm at Hamim in 2013.

By Jung Da-hyun
Published KST
Updated KST
Scorching weather to persist this week
Visitors crowd Haeundae Beach in Busan amid a record-breaking heat wave, Sunday. Nearby, Yangsan in South Gyeongsang Province, recorded a high of 42.5 degrees Celsius the same day, the highest temperature ever recorded in Korea's 122 years of modern weather observation. Newsis
Yangsan, South Gyeongsang Province, recorded a temperature of 42.5 degrees Celsius on Sunday, the highest ever measured in Korea since modern weather observation began in 1904, as a record-breaking heat wave grips the country.
The temperature was recorded at approximately 1:26 p.m. The southeastern city set a new local temperature record for a fourth straight day since Wednesday, with temperatures climbing higher each day.
Daytime temperatures also topped 40 degrees in other areas, including northern Busan, Gimhae in South Gyeongsang Province, Gyeongju in North Gyeongsang Province, and Gwangyang in South Jeolla Province.
At 11 a.m., the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) upgraded the heat wave advisory for northwestern Seoul to a heat wave warning, placing all of the capital under the second highest-level heat alert. Heat wave warnings had already been in effect for southeastern, southwestern and northeastern Seoul since Wednesday.
As the prolonged heat wave continued across the country, the government raised the Central Disaster and Safety Countermeasures Headquarters to Level 2, stepping up nationwide response efforts with expanded field inspections and financial support.
Gwangalli Beach in Busan's Suyeong District appears relatively quiet because of record-breaking heat, Thursday. Yonhap
According to the KMA, a rare combination of large-scale weather patterns and local geographic conditions fueled the extreme heat that engulfed Yangsan and other parts of South Gyeongsang Province.
Overlapping high-pressure systems over the Korean Peninsula created ideal conditions for the heat wave. The North Pacific High, a semipermanent anticyclone, brought hot, humid air, while the Tibetan High, a seasonal high-pressure system that forms over the Tibetan plateau, reinforced atmospheric warming to produce clear skies and intense sunshine that drove temperatures even higher.
Dry conditions left by below-average monsoon rainfall also intensified the heat, while the stagnant weather pattern allowed it to build across the southeast.
Local geography further amplified the heat in Yangsan. Surrounded by mountains, the city is in a basin that traps heat and limits air circulation, which allowed temperatures to climb to record levels.
Water is sprayed over spectators during a baseball game between the Kiwoom Heroes and LG Twins at Jamsil Baseball Stadium in Seoul during a record-breaking heat wave, Wednesday. Yonhap
The prolonged heat wave continued to cause casualties and disruptions across the country.
According to the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, 1,871 cases of heat-related illnesses were reported between May 15 and July 31, including 13 deaths.
The scorching temperatures also disrupted professional baseball across southern region. Korean Baseball Organization League games in Changwon, South Gyeongsang Province, were canceled on both Saturday and Sunday after forecasts showed temperatures would be above 38 degrees at first pitch.
In Busan, Saturday's game was canceled, while Sunday's game was rescheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m., 30 minutes later than originally planned, to avoid the worst of the heat.
Meanwhile, sweltering temperatures are expected to persist this week, with daytime highs forecast to reach as high as 38 degrees in some areas.
The KMA said heat wave conditions and tropical nights are likely to continue across most of the country, with the heat index expected to exceed 33 degrees in most regions and 35 degrees in inland areas.
Under the continued influence of the North Pacific High, most of the country is expected to see clear skies throughout the week. Morning lows will range from 23 to 27 degrees , while daytime highs are forecast at 32 to 37 degrees — about 3 to 4 degrees above the seasonal average.

Temperatures soared to a record high of 42.5 C in the southeastern city of Yangsan on Sunday, as a scorching heat wave continues to grip Korea, the state weather agency said.
The mercury reached 42 C in Yangsan, about 310 kilometers southeast of Seoul, at 1:16 p.m. and further rose to 42.5 C at 1:26 p.m., according to the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA).
It marked the highest reading since modern weather observations began on the Korean Peninsula in 1904, based on records from the KMA's 97 long-term observation stations.
The timing of the temperature rising above 40 C in Yangsan has been occurring earlier each day, as heat continues to accumulate, raising concerns the temperature could even surpass 43 C.
Sunday marked the fifth straight day temperatures exceeded 40 C in the southeastern city.

Temperatures had also risen to 40.2 C in Gyeongju, about 240 kilometers southeast of Seoul, as of 1:55 p.m., marking the first time the mercury rose above 40 C in the city this year.
It was the highest temperature reported in eight years after the mercury hit 39.8 C in 2018.
The government issued a "Level 2" emergency operation of the disaster response headquarters as of 1 p.m. to strengthen the government-wide response to the extreme heat.
It also advised the public to refrain from outdoor activities and abide by safety measures.
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook issued emergency orders for government ministries and provincial governments to strengthen safety checks on people who are most vulnerable to the heat, and to maintain stable power and water supply.

Heatstroke Cases Triple in Five Years as Fatal Heat Illness Surges
Culture||
By Kim Yeo-jin
||
Amid a record-breaking heat wave, heatstroke, the most fatal among heat-related illnesses, has more than tripled over the past five years. With most of this year's heat-related deaths presumed to be caused by heatstroke, experts stressed that early symptoms should not be dismissed as merely "overheating" and that emergency measures to lower body temperature are needed immediately.
Tripled in Five Years... Most Heat-Related Deaths from Heatstroke
According to the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service on the 2nd, the number of heatstroke patients in Korea rose nearly fivefold in five years, from 1,073 in 2020 to 5,529 last year. Over the same period, the number of hospital visit days increased 163.6% from 4,068 to 10,725, and total medical benefit costs rose 277.3% from 1.07 billion won to 4.04 billion won.
Heatstroke is a representative severe heat-related illness that occurs when the body's temperature regulation function collapses after prolonged exposure to extreme heat. Unlike heat exhaustion, heat syncope, or heat cramps, it can raise the core body temperature to around 40 degrees and be accompanied by central nervous system abnormalities such as reduced consciousness, delirium, and convulsions. Even if the body temperature does not reach 40 degrees, heatstroke should be suspected if changes in consciousness appear.
In fact, about 44% of heatstroke patients from 2011 to 2025 showed symptoms such as impaired or lost consciousness. In contrast, more than 90% of patients with heat exhaustion, heat cramps, and heat syncope were found to have clear consciousness.
The fatality rate is also overwhelmingly high. According to the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency's emergency room heat illness surveillance system, 256 of the 267 heat-related deaths from 2011 to 2025 (95.8%) died from heatstroke. Heatstroke accounted for 21.6% of all heat-related illnesses, but its mortality rate was 4.4%, more than 100 times higher than heat exhaustion (0.04%). This year as well, all 13 presumed heat-related deaths as of the 30th of last month were estimated to have been affected by heatstroke, and 11 of them (84.6%) were aged 65 or older.
Dismissing It as "Overheating" Is Dangerous... Call 119 in These Cases
Heatstroke initially begins with mild symptoms such as fatigue, headache, and dizziness, but if left untreated, it can threaten life within a short time. If you tire more easily than usual, feel weak, or experience a heavy head, dizziness, or staggering, you should immediately rest in a cool place and replenish fluids sufficiently.
"When exposed to heat for a long time, blood rushes toward the skin to lower body temperature, reducing blood flow to the brain," said Kim Han-bit, a professor of emergency medicine at Soonchunhyang University Bucheon Hospital. "This can cause dizziness or reduced consciousness."
Although heat exhaustion and heatstroke may look similar, their dangers differ greatly. "Heat exhaustion is the condition commonly described as 'being overheated,' involving excessive sweating along with thirst, weakness, and dizziness," said Kim Won-hee, a professor of emergency medicine at Hallym University Kangnam Sacred Heart Hospital. "In contrast, heatstroke is an emergency illness in which the hypothalamus function that regulates body temperature is damaged, causing body temperature to rise sharply and even accompanied by reduced consciousness."
If the skin is hot and red but there is little sweat, or if consciousness becomes cloudy, heatstroke should be suspected immediately. "If heatstroke is suspected, with body temperature rising above 40 degrees and consciousness declining, you should call 119 right away," Professor Kim Han-bit stressed. "It is important to move the patient to a shaded or air-conditioned place, loosen their clothing, and then spray cool water or use a fan to lower their body temperature as quickly as possible."
He added, "On days when a heat wave warning is issued, avoid outdoor activities as much as possible, and if going out is unavoidable, it is better to use the early morning or evening hours. It is also necessary to develop the habit of drinking water frequently before feeling thirsty and blocking direct sunlight with a parasol or hat."

Heatstroke Cases Surge Fivefold in Five Years, Elderly Most at Risk
Heatstroke Accounts for 95.8% of Heat-Related Deaths
"Fatigue, Headache, Dizziness Are Early Symptoms"
Society||
By Kim Eun-bi
||
Heatstroke cases have surged more than fivefold over the past five years, according to data.
The number of heatstroke patients rose 415.3% from 1,073 in 2020 to 5,529 last year, according to the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service on the 2nd. Over the same period, hospital visit days for heatstroke patients jumped 163.6% from 4,068 to 10,725, while total medical care benefit costs surged 277.3% from 1.07 billion won to 4.04 billion won.
Heatstroke is among the most severe of heat-related illnesses. Prolonged exposure to high temperatures raises core body temperature above 40 degrees Celsius, causing central nervous system abnormalities such as altered consciousness, delirium and seizures.
Indeed, about 44% of heatstroke patients between 2011 and 2025 experienced changes in consciousness, including impaired consciousness (31.1%), loss of consciousness (11.6%) and death (1.4%). By contrast, more than 90% of patients with heat exhaustion, heat cramps and heat syncope remained fully conscious.
Heatstroke can lead to death if not treated promptly. Of the 267 heat-related deaths recorded between 2011 and 2025 through the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency's emergency room heat illness surveillance system, 256, or 95.8%, died from heatstroke.
During this period, heatstroke patients accounted for 21.6% of all heat illness patients, with a fatality rate of 4.4%. This is far higher than the fatality rate of heat exhaustion (0.04%), a relatively mild condition.
As of the 30th of last month, heatstroke is also presumed to have contributed to this year's 13 estimated heat-related deaths. Notably, 11 of the 13 deaths (84.6%), excluding two, were elderly people aged 65 or older.
Heatstroke begins with mild symptoms but can worsen rapidly depending on the person and circumstances. The first warning sign is excessive fatigue. A person may tire more easily than usual, lose energy and struggle even with simple activities. At this point, adequate rest and hydration can prevent symptoms from worsening.
Headache and dizziness are also major early symptoms. Patients may complain that their "head feels heavy," that they feel "dizzy" or that their "vision is blurred," while losing their sense of balance and staggering. As body temperature rises in earnest, the skin becomes hot and red, and sweating may actually cease almost entirely.
"Heatstroke is unlikely unless one is exposed to an extremely hot environment," said Kim Jun-sung, a professor of emergency medicine at Asan Medical Center. "When a heat wave advisory is issued, avoid going outside as much as possible, and if you must go out, use the early morning or late evening hours."

Orange alert issued for 12 Kerala districts
The orange alert has been issued for Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod districts.According to the IMD, an orange alert signifies the possibility of very heavy rainfall ranging between 115.6 mm and 204.4 mm within 24 hours at isolated places.

KSDMA issues safety advisory amid heavy rain
As heavy rain continued to cause landslides and flooding, the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) urged residents in areas vulnerable to landslides, mudslides and flash floods to move to safer places if instructed by authorities.People living along riverbanks and downstream of dams were advised to remain alert and relocate if directed by officials. The authority also asked residents in disaster-prone areas to ensure relief camps had been opened in their localities and to shift there during the daytime if necessary.
The KSDMA further advised those living in weak or unsafe houses to exercise caution due to the possibility of strong winds and move to safer locations if required.
Public urged to avoid water bodies and unnecessary travel
The disaster management authority cautioned people against entering rivers, streams and other water bodies for bathing, fishing or crossing during the heavy rainfall.It also advised the public not to gather on bridges or attempt to take photographs or selfies near overflowing water bodies.
People have been urged to avoid all non-essential travel, especially to hilly areas, waterfalls and reservoirs, until the weather warning is withdrawn.
Examinations postponed across Kerala
The General Education Department postponed the State Eligibility Test scheduled for August 2 due to the prevailing heavy rain. It said the revised examination date would be announced later and advised candidates to regularly check the official website for updates.The department also postponed the Higher Secondary Equivalency Examination scheduled for August 2 because of heavy rain and the resulting disruptions across the state. Fresh dates will be announced later.
Meanwhile, Mahatma Gandhi University in Kottayam postponed all examinations scheduled for August 3 owing to the prevailing weather conditions. The university said revised dates would be notified later.
Kerala PSC offers relief to affected candidates
The Kerala Public Service Commission announced that candidates from flood and landslide-affected areas who could not appear for competitive examinations conducted on Saturday would be given another opportunity to take the examinations.The announcements came as heavy rain continued to trigger landslides and flooding across several districts, affecting transportation and disrupting normal life throughout the state.
